intent.purpose: The per-session channel through which a session reports its lifecycle changes to the distributor's session catalog (Sessions API): session created; run started or ended with outcome and failed steps; ask opened, resolved or cancelled; artifact sealed; spend; title; state. One operation — POST /sessions/{key}/events on the credentialed session listener — takes batches of events derived from the session's own durable log, authenticated by the session's launch credential, ordered by a per-session sequence number and acked by a watermark. The session's log is the outbox: while the distributor is down, events wait in the log and replay on reconnect, and replaying the whole log recovers the session's rows. The channel replaces the index's fact publishing (POST /index/facts), deleted with the index package, and feeds the notifications adapter that takes over index.push's notification behaviour.
nonGoals: The catalog and its reads and person writes (rename, resolve, archive, delete): the Sessions API contract (quack v2), which defers this channel as 'specified separately' and records what the catalog stores as a result.
index.push (web push): its routes and payloads stay their own contract; this channel only carries what that notifications adapter needs.
The catalog rebuild itself: an internal recovery operation of the distributor, not an API; the channel provides the replay it rides on.

State writes a person makes: archived/stopped and title via PATCH /sessions/{key}, ask resolution via PATCH /sessions/{key}/asks/{id} — those are written by the Sessions API, not reported here (the session reports the resolutions it itself recorded).
Session transcripts, messages, sockets and invocations: those routes drive the session's process and are not part of this channel.
Cross-session reporting: a launch credential never reports another session's key.
intent.audience: Internal to one quack deployment: every session process talks to its own distributor's credentialed session listener.
consumers: Every session process — the runtime publisher that today posts index facts to {QUACK_INDEX_URL}/index/facts, targeting this route instead with the same launch token (QUACK_INDEX_TOKEN)
The distributor — applies each batch to the session catalog (SQLite by default, Postgres when the deployment configures it)
The distributor's notifications adapter — the successor to index.push's notification behaviour, fed by the same applied events
guarantees: Per-session authentication: the session's launch credential, minted per launch and revoked when the session process exits, on the credentialed session listener #2220 introduces; a credential reaches only its own key — 404 on a foreign key, 401 on a missing, unknown or revoked one.

Idempotency: a stable event id plus a per-session sequence number; a retried batch applies nothing twice, an event at or below the catalog's watermark is skipped, and a higher seq with the same id supersedes the earlier one, so an older revision never overwrites a newer one.

The log is the outbox: unsent events are the derived events beyond the last ack; a crash, an outage or a restart loses nothing, and a down distributor simply holds them in the session's log until reconnect.

Deterministic replay: the event stream is a pure function of the session's log, so replaying the whole log — triggered implicitly when the distributor's watermark drops — converges to the same state as live publishing.
At most one event stale: a catalog row reflects the session's latest applied events (Sessions API).

Errors are application/problem+json; 401 and 400 are permanent (the session logs them and does not retry the same body), 409 carries the watermark to resync, 413 splits the batch, and 503 and timeouts retry on bounded backoff.
Money is never a float: spend is { currencyCode, amountMicros }, an int64 count of millionths encoded as a decimal string.

info.title: Quack session lifecycle channel
info.description:
The Sessions API's deferred channel: one session reports its lifecycle changes to the distributor's session catalog — session created; run started or ended with outcome and failed steps; ask opened, resolved or cancelled; artifact sealed; spend; title; state. This replaces the index's fact publishing (POST /index/facts), which is deleted with the whole index package: the distributor keeps no index store; it writes the catalog (SQLite by default, Postgres when configured) directly.

Transport: REST on the separate credentialed session listener #2220 introduces, apart from the person/proxy listener. One operation: POST /sessions/{key}/events. A batch POST is the house pattern — the session already holds a per-launch credential minted for exactly this boundary (the distributor mints QUACK_INDEX_TOKEN at launch and revokes it when the process exits) and already publishes to the distributor over plain HTTP — and it keeps the distributor a pure push receiver that never has to reach the session's process, which does not exist while the session is stopped.

Identity and ordering: every event carries a stable `id` — derived from the session's log, so the same logical event re-derives with the same id — and a per-session strictly increasing `seq`, an ordinal in the session's derived event stream. Within a batch, `seq` strictly increases. The catalog keeps one watermark per session, the highest seq it has applied. The distributor applies a batch in seq order, skips events at or below the watermark (a retried batch applies nothing twice), answers 409 carrying the watermark when a batch starts more than one past it, and answers 200 with the new watermark. An event with the same id at a higher seq supersedes the earlier one (spend, state and run outcome derive cumulatively), so an older revision never overwrites a newer one.

Outbox and outage: the session's own durable log is the outbox. The session derives its event set from the log; its unsent set is the derived events with seq beyond the last ack, so a crash, an outage or a restart loses nothing. While the distributor is down, events wait in the log: the publisher retries on bounded backoff (503 and timeouts retry; 401 and 400 are logged as permanent and not retried as the same body; 413 splits the batch at a seq boundary, which is safe because resume is seq-driven).

Replay and recovery: the event stream is a deterministic function of the session's log — replaying the log yields the same events as live publishing. Whole-log replay needs no operation of its own: every 200 carries the watermark, so when the distributor is rebuilt and its watermark resets, the session sees the drop on its next flush and re-sends from seq 0. The catalog rebuild that orchestrates this across sessions is an internal distributor operation, not an API (a Sessions API non-goal).

Notifications: the distributor's notifications adapter — the successor to index.push's notification behaviour, whose web push routes and payloads stay a separate contract — is fed by these same applied events: ask.opened (the approval's toolCall.args or the question's prompt), run.ended (an outcome of failed wakes a phone, and a run's end is when versions that will never get a verdict are found among the session's artifacts), artifact.sealed (its verdict), title.set (the notification's title) and each event's `at` (an event older than six hours is a replay or a long outage catching up, not news).

Cutover: the index package is deleted when this channel ships. The runtime publisher that today posts facts to {QUACK_INDEX_URL}/index/facts with QUACK_INDEX_TOKEN targets POST /sessions/{key}/events instead, with the same launch token. v1 facts ({id, kind, rev, at, data}) become events ({seq, id, at, type, data}): kind 'session' → session.created; 'status' → run.started, run.ended and state.changed; 'approval' and 'question' → ask.opened, ask.resolved and ask.cancelled; 'artifact' → artifact.sealed; 'failure' folds into run.ended.failedSteps; 'cost' → spend.recorded. Money is { currencyCode, amountMicros } (ISO 4217; int64 millionths as a decimal string), never a float. The route is unversioned and is mounted at the deployment's root (locally) or under /v1/ behind the reverse proxy, exactly as today.

post.description: One batch of this session's derived lifecycle events, in seq order. The key must be the credential's own session: a launch credential reaches only its own key and answers 404 on a foreign one. Rules: `events[].seq` strictly increases within the batch; the first event's seq must be at most one past the catalog's watermark for this session, else the reply is 409 whose problem body carries the watermark as `acked`, and the session resumes from there; events at or below the watermark are skipped, so a retried batch applies nothing twice; an event with the same id at a higher seq supersedes the earlier one. A successful batch answers 200 with { acked }, the highest applied seq — the session's outbox is its derived events beyond it. Batches cap at 500 events, and a body over the 1 MiB limit answers 413, which the session answers by splitting the batch at a seq boundary. The session reports only what it observes: state.changed is running or idle — stopped and archived are set by the distributor itself (a process it stopped, the retention sweep) or through the Sessions API (PATCH /sessions/{key}). An ask resolved through the Sessions API is written there directly; the ask.resolved events this channel carries are the resolutions the session itself recorded, and their `by` is the Principal the session saw (the person behind the session route's identity header, or the tailnet), never a value invented from the request.

parameters.name: key
parameters.description: The session key. Must be the credential's own session: the listener answers 404 for a foreign key, never 403 — the key is an object boundary the credential may not reach, not a permission it lacks.

200.description: The batch was applied in seq order, events at or below the watermark skipped, and each applied event superseding any earlier one with its id. `acked` is this session's new watermark — the highest applied seq — and the session's outbox is its derived events beyond it.

400.description: The batch is malformed: not an object, events not an array of well-formed events, a seq not a positive integer, a seq not strictly increasing within the batch, or an unknown event type. Permanent for the session — it logs the rejection and does not retry the same body.

401.description: The credential is missing, unknown or revoked (the launch is over, so its token is). Permanent for the session — a launch credential never recovers by retrying.

404.description: The key is not the credential's own session: a launch credential reaches only its own key. Permanent for the session — a credential is never granted another session's key on this channel.

409.description: A gap: the batch's first seq is more than one past the catalog's watermark for this session. The problem body carries the watermark as `acked`; the session resumes from there (its log is the outbox, so the missing events are still in it).

413.description: The body is over the 1 MiB limit. The session splits the batch at a seq boundary and re-sends the halves — safe because resume is seq-driven and the halves share the watermark.

503.description: The catalog is unavailable (the store is down). The session retries on bounded backoff; the events wait in the session's log, which is the outbox.

default.description: An unexpected error; the session retries on bounded backoff, as for 503.

session.description: The session's launch credential: an opaque token the distributor mints for each launch of the session and revokes when the session process exits. On the credentialed session listener #2220 introduces, it reaches only its own session's key — a POST for any other key answers 404 — and a missing, unknown or revoked credential answers 401. This channel has no cross-session grant: a credential never reports another session's events (the Sessions API's home-agent grant covers reads there, not reporting here).

events.description: The batch, in strictly increasing seq order. The cap keeps one request under the 1 MiB body limit; above it the reply is 413 and the session splits at a seq boundary.

Event.description: One lifecycle event of a session: a stable `id` (derived from the session's log, so re-derivation — replay included — yields the same id), a per-session strictly increasing `seq` (its ordinal in the derived stream), an RFC 3339 `at`, its `type`, and the typed `data`. An event with the same id at a higher seq supersedes the earlier one, so an older revision never overwrites a newer one.

EventSessionCreated.description: The session exists: its key is the path's, its identity is here. Reported once, first in the stream.

seq.description: The event's ordinal in the session's derived stream; strictly increasing per session.

agent.description: The agent bound to the session.

version.description: The agent's version, when the definition carries one.

createdAt.description: When the session was created (RFC 3339); the catalog row's createdAt.

EventRunStarted.description: The session began a run: state moves to running and any asks pending into the run are the run's to answer or cancel.

run.description: The run's number within the session, starting at 1.

EventRunEnded.description: The session's current run ended: the catalog's lastRun { outcome, endedAt, failedSteps } is written from it (endedAt is the event's `at`), and the asks the run raised that are still pending are cancelled by it.

run.description: The run's number within the session.

failedSteps.description: The run's steps that ended failed, with their error text; empty on a clean run. This is the catalog row's lastRun.failedSteps.

EventAskOpened.description: The session raised an ask — approval or question, the Sessions API's one Ask type — moving it to pending. The data is the Ask's fields apart from state, which the catalog sets to pending.

AskOpenedData.description: The Ask's fields apart from state: toolCall is present for type approval and prompt for type question, so the notifications adapter sees what waits without touching the session.

id.description: The ask's id within its session.

type.description: What kind of ask: a gated tool call, or a prompt to a person.

createdAt.description: When the ask was raised (RFC 3339); the catalog's oldestAskAt while pending.

ToolCall.description: The gated tool call; present for type approval, and kept by the catalog after resolution — the record of what was approved.

args.description: The gated arguments, retained on resolution. A summary member, when present, is what the notifications adapter shows.

Prompt.description: The prompt; present for type question.

question.description: The question text; what the notifications adapter shows.

optionDescriptions.description: A per-option description, keyed by the option's label.

freeText.description: Whether a free-text answer was allowed.

header.description: A short chip naming the topic.

EventAskResolved.description: The session recorded an answer to one of its asks (a person through the session's own routes). An ask resolved through the Sessions API is written there directly and does not come over this channel.

AskResolvedData.description: The answer. `by` is the Principal the session itself recorded from whoever answered in its own UI — the person behind the session route's identity header, or the tailnet — and the distributor stores it as given; the channel's credential is the session, not the resolver, so it is not the request's credential as on the Sessions API's PATCH.

id.description: The ask's id within its session.

choice.description: The chosen option's label, or approve/reject for an approval ask.

text.description: A free-text answer; present when the prompt offered freeText.

EventAskCancelled.description: An ask the session raised is cancelled — because the run that raised it ended or aborted, which is what keeps the catalog's pendingAsks from leaking.

id.description: The ask's id within its session.

run.description: The run that ended or aborted, cancelling it.

EventArtifactSealed.description: The session sealed an artifact version; the catalog's artifact row is written from it (createdAt is the event's `at`). The notifications adapter reads the verdict from it, so a run's end can find versions that will never get one.

sealedAt.description: When the version was sealed; defaults to the event's `at`.

verdict.description: The judge's verdict, when the version was checked; null while unchecked. A higher seq with the same event id supersedes with the verdict filled in.

summary.description: A one-line summary of the version.

Verdict.description: The judge's verdict, when the version was checked.

limitReached.description: The judge released it unpassed after its revision limit.

EventSpendRecorded.description: The session's spend, as cumulative totals since the session's start — never per-call deltas — so a later seq with the same id simply supersedes and the catalog row's cost and tokens always show the whole session. Unpriced spend is amountMicros "0", never absent.

id.description: The event's stable id, e.g. `spend` — one logical quantity, superseded in place.

Money.description: A money amount, google.type.Money style: never a float, so nothing loses precision in JavaScript. Unpriced spend is amountMicros "0" with the deployment's currency, never null.

currencyCode.description: ISO 4217 currency code — the deployment's currency.

amountMicros.description: An int64 count of millionths of the currency unit, encoded as a decimal string so values past 2^53 survive JavaScript clients; "1250000" is 1.25 of the unit.

Tokens.description: Tokens by kind, cumulative since the session's start; always present.

EventTitleSet.description: The session's display title changed: the default derived from the session's first message, or the title an invocation carried. A person's rename through the Sessions API is written there directly.

id.description: The event's stable id, e.g. `title` — one logical quantity, superseded in place.

title.description: The session's title; at most 120 characters.

EventStateChanged.description: The session observed its own lifecycle state: running when a run starts (or it waits on a person) and idle when it ends. Only these two values come over the channel — stopped is set by the distributor when the process stops, and archived through the Sessions API — so a session never reports a state it cannot observe.

id.description: The event's stable id, one per occurrence, e.g. `state:15`.

state.description: The state the session observed: running or idle — never stopped or archived, which are set by the distributor or the Sessions API.

Principal.description: Who an ask's answer came from, as the session recorded it: `person` when the answer arrived with a trusted identity (the session route's identity header), `tailnet` when it did not. On this channel it is data the session reports about itself — the channel's credential is the session, not the resolver.

id.description: The person's username; present when kind is person, absent when kind is tailnet.

acked.description: This session's new watermark: the highest seq the catalog has applied. The session's outbox is its derived events beyond it; a watermark lower than the session's own last ack means the catalog was reset, and the session re-sends from seq 0.

Problem.description: An RFC 9457 problem; `error` repeats `detail` for readers that predate problem+json. On 409 the problem carries the session's current watermark as `acked`, so the session resumes from it without another round trip.

acked.description: Present on 409 only: this session's current watermark, where the session resumes.
